message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel numeric work – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific, machine‑learning, and other highly parallel tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each core is powerful, with deep pipelines, large caches, complex control logic, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution. | Hundreds or thousands of lightweight cores, optimized for throughput rather than single‑thread latency. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) or reduced instruction set (RISC) with many features (branch prediction, speculative execution). | Simpler, often SIMD‑style instructions; many cores execute the same instruction on different data (SIMD/streaming). |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated memory controllers, high cache coherence protocols. | Smaller per‑core caches, rely on high bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory pools. |
| **Latency vs Throughput** | Optimized for low latency – quick response to individual threads. | Optimized for high throughput – many operations per cycle across many threads. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control flow heavy, branching, I/O bound, small data sets, single‑thread performance critical. | Data‑parallel, compute‑heavy, floating‑point intensive, large data sets, embarrassingly parallel problems. |
| **Programming Model** | Single‑threaded or multi‑threaded with OS scheduling, standard languages (C/C++, Java, etc.). | Parallel programming models (CUDA, OpenCL, DirectX, Vulkan, Metal, etc.) or higher‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |
| **Energy Efficiency** | More power per core, but fewer cores overall. | Many cores share resources, can be more energy efficient for parallel workloads. |

In short, a CPU is a generalist with strong single‑thread performance and complex control logic, while a GPU is a specialist that excels at performing the same operation on many pieces of data simultaneously. That’s why GPUs have become popular for machine learning, scientific simulations, and other workloads that fit their massively parallel architecture.
